newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: COFFEE -- ACPC to push for expanded membership.
newsitem.headline: COFFEE -- ACPC to push for expanded membership.

text.p: The Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC) will push to expand its membership and tighten control over world supply at next week's meeting in London, Colombia's coffee czar said.

Jorge Cardenas, head of the powerful National Coffee Growers Federation, said winning over countries like Mexico and Guatemala that have kept to the sidelines of the ACPC was critical to the success of its retention plan aimed at driving up world prices.
"All of us have made a very great effort to defend prices by controlling supply and ensuring market discipline every way possible," Cardenas told Reuters in an interview this week.
"But this effort can be very frustrating and limiting if all producers don't participate in it," he said.
Cardenas said at the moment, the 14-member ACPC represents about 75 percent of world's coffee growing countries.

But in addition to Mexico and Guatemala, he said the membership of producers like Vietnam, India and New Guinea was needed to give the association's efforts to dictate supply levels "more solidity and credibility."

Cardenas did not elaborate on what specific measures might be used by ACPC member countries to convince independent producer countries to join it. But he said the time had come for efforts to be made through "high-level officials or presidents."
At the ACPC's meeting in May, member countries agreed to limit their total green coffee exports to 53.5 million 60-kilo bags between July 1996 and June 1997.
Cardenas ruled out any bid to change that plan at next week's meeting, even though it has failed to give prices much of a jolt so far.
"The program covering July 1996 to June 1997 has already been agreed," he said. "The idea is to fulfill it and not be modifying it and sending out different signals to the market."
Apart from efforts to broaden the ACPC's membership, the London meeting will focus on "production and marketing policies for the new (1996-1997) coffee year," Cardenas said.
"We're going to study the current price situation and what sort of problems are surfacing in the market that may need to be analyzed in the future," he said.
